blocks.text: When teams are going from prototype to production faster than ever, it’s easy for important context to get lost along the way. Written requirements, design details, and engineering guidance are critical to making sure teams are sprinting toward the right outcomes, but these inputs often end up scattered across separate documents and links.

blocks.text: The problem

inlines.text: The problem

blocks.text: The team at Pickup, a fictional marketplace shopping app, is scoping a new delivery feature. The lead engineer is taking stock of the designs and technical decisions they’ll need to build it: There’s a PRD, a diagram in FigJam, and a Figma file containing designs, code layersDesign together with code layers on the canvasToday, code layers moves into open beta. Now teams can explore and build prototypes backed by code on the canvas., and components on the canvas. Across all of these sources, it’s not clear which details are missing or who still needs to give input. The engineer needs to connect the dots.

blocks.text: Starting with the data

inlines.text: Starting with the data

blocks.text: The engineer combs through the PRD and notices that the team plans to pilot the new delivery feature in a single city, but haven’t identified which one yet. The engineer doesn’t want to start implementing code until they know which city’s map they’re building for, so they decide to look into where Pickup’s demand is highest based on the app’s usage data. That data lives in Hex, the team’s data analytics platform, but the engineer wants designers and other teammates to be able to view and react to the data in a shared space.

blocks.text: Connectors let the agent access information from a tool outside Figma.

inlines.text: Connectors

blocks.text: The engineer turns to the Figma agent to help add the data to the canvas in the form of a spec. They open the agent, add the Hex connector to the conversation, and prompt: Go find where we have the most usage of Pickup and create a spec breaking that down. Also, update this map code layer to show usage data for the top cities.

blocks.text: The product team’s PRD sits in a spec beside a map code layer, keeping the delivery requirements alongside the working prototype.

inlines.text: The product team’s PRD sits in a spec beside a map code layer, keeping the delivery requirements alongside the working prototype.

blocks.text: The agent produces a spec that contains a table with app usage and order volume by city, along with code layers showing maps for each of the top four cities. The engineer and their collaborators review the Hex data and the screens on the canvas. The team decides to launch in Bengaluru, India, the city that clearly has the highest density of customers and demand.

blocks.text: Gathering context on the canvas

inlines.text: Gathering context on the canvas

blocks.text: The engineer opens the team’s technical spec. It explains how the app will store information about deliveries, how the team will make the feature available to customers, and how they’ll monitor it for problems after launch. They then drag in an existing FigJam diagram showing the delivery process and what the seller, buyer, and driver each do.

blocks.text: The engineer embeds the delivery lifecycle diagram in the technical spec, bringing the visual explanation together with the written requirements.

blocks.text: Elsewhere on the canvas, designers are reviewing the final screens. The team has added annotations on the frames to call out key details, and both design and engineering approved the designs.

blocks.text: The team specifies when to show the delivery icon and reminds developers to display prices in the local currency.

blocks.text: The engineer also includes an interactive version of the Bengaluru map as a code layer so the agent can see how it should work—for example, how nearby items group together and how they animate as someone moves around the map.

blocks.text: Lastly, the engineer reviews a new component from the design systems team. A code layer shows how the component works, and a written spec beside it explains when to use it instead of the existing component.

blocks.text: The engineer selects the technical spec, annotated design frames, interactive map code layer, new component, and design system guidance on the canvas, then opens the Figma agent. They prompt the team’s previously configured build-implementation-plan skill—a reusable set of instructions for the agent. The agent creates a new spec that brings those inputs together into a plan for a coding agent to build the feature, including how it should look and behave.

blocks.text: Reviewing the plan and handing it off

inlines.text: Reviewing the plan and handing it off

blocks.text: Before handing the plan off to a coding agent, the engineer reviews it to make sure the details are right, expanding the spec to its full width. They check that the spec includes the team’s design system, testing and observability requirements, rollout details, and a table outlining what needs to be done to build and ship the feature, along with references back to the specs, designs, and code layers it draws from.

blocks.text: The agent creates a spec with an implementation plan for the engineer to review before handing it to a coding agent.

blocks.text: The engineer spots a detail in the spec that isn’t quite right, leaves a comment on the spec with the problem, then prompts the Figma agent: Read my comment and reply to it with a solution. The agent comments back with an edit for the engineer to review. Reading on, the engineer notices another detail that needs adjustment, but this one requires input from a designer on the team, who the engineer tags in a comment. The designer receives a notification, jumps into the spec, and makes the change in real time.

blocks.text: The TL;DR on MCP: Why context matters and how to put it to workFigma’s MCP server brings your design decisions into the tools where code gets written—so what gets built actually matches what was designed. Here’s what that unlocks for everyone who builds products., Codex can read not just the spec, but also the annotated design frames, code layers, design system components, and other context that went into the plan—all with just one link. All of that context helps Codex build the delivery feature, and once implemented, the team can review and test the feature before rolling it out to users.
